data.heading: Legal System Development During Soviet Period
bullets: 28 people's courts were closed due to personnel shortage
Tashkent Law Institute resumed operations in 1942 after being suspended in 1941
Four-month courses opened in Tashkent and six-month courses in Samarkand in August 1943
By end of 1945, only 56 lawyers with higher education remained in people's courts

narr: During the Soviet period, Uzbekistan faced significant challenges in its legal system.
The closure of 28 people's courts created a severe personnel shortage.
To address this, educational initiatives were implemented.
The Tashkent Law Institute, which had been suspended in 1941, resumed operations in 1942.
In August 1943, specialized courses were established in Tashkent and Samarkand.
Despite these efforts, by the end of 1945, only 56 lawyers with higher education remained in the people's courts.

data.title: Four Stages of Legal System Development
data.subtitle: Independent Uzbekistan

narr: Following independence, Uzbekistan's legal system evolved through distinct stages.
N. P. Azizov identifies four key periods in this development.

data.heading: Stage 1 (1991–2000): Transitional Period
bullets: Formation of foundations of national statehood
Emergence of new branches of law

narr: The first stage from 1991 to 2000 was a transitional period focused on establishing the foundations of national statehood.
This included the adoption of the constitutional law on August 31, 1991, which contained 17 articles.
A new Constitution was adopted to establish the framework for the new nation.
During this time, new branches of law began to emerge.
The foundation was laid with 15 codes established between 1994 and 2008.

data.heading: Stage 2 (2001–2009): Democratic Renewal
bullets: Transfer of arrest sanctions to courts (2007)
Reclassification of 75% of serious crimes as less serious
20% reduction in sentences by 2006 compared to 2000

narr: The second stage from 2001 to 2009 focused on democratic renewal.
Key developments included the establishment of a bicameral parliament.
The death penalty was abolished during this period.
In 2007, arrest sanctions were transferred to the courts.
Significant legal reforms led to the reclassification of 75% of serious crimes as less serious.
By 2006, there was a 20% reduction in sentences compared to 2000.
The third stage from 2010 to 2016 focused on deepening democratic reforms.
During this period, approximately fifty new laws were enacted.
These reforms continued the development of democratic institutions.
The legal framework was further strengthened during this phase.

data.heading: Stage 4 (Since 2017): Strategy of Actions
bullets: Creation of Supreme Council of Judges
Judicial appointment system: 5 years, then 10 years, then for life

narr: The fourth stage beginning in 2017 is defined by the Strategy of Actions.
Judicial reform was established as the second priority in this strategy.
The Supreme Council of Judges was created to oversee the judiciary.
A unified Supreme Court was established to centralize judicial authority.
The system included the formation of 71 economic courts.
The judicial appointment system was structured in phases: initially for 5 years, then 10 years, and finally for life.
Torture was explicitly prohibited during this stage.

data.heading: Question 1: Constitution Adoption

steps.text: The Constitution was adopted on December 8, 1992
Adopted by the eleventh session of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Legally formalized the formation of a new sovereign democratic state
Created as the fruit and product of state independence
Deputies made about 80 amendments, additions, and clarifications

data.result: The first Constitution was adopted on December 8, 1992 by the Supreme Council, formalizing Uzbekistan's independence as a sovereign democratic state.

narr: Let's examine the first question about the adoption of Uzbekistan's Constitution.
When was the first Constitution adopted?
It was adopted on December 8, 1992.
By which body was it adopted?
It was adopted by the eleventh session of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Uzbekistan.
In what context was it adopted?
It legally formalized the formation of a new sovereign democratic state on the world map.
The first President I. A. Karimov called it 'a manifesto of our freedom and security'.

data.heading: Question 2: Constitutional Commission
data.problem: How was the Constitutional Commission formed and how did it work?

steps.text: Created after adoption of Declaration of Independence (June 20, 1990)
Initially formed by Supreme Council session with 64 people chaired by I. A. Karimov
Composition updated to 71 members on July 2–3, 1992
Direct work began April 12, 1991 with working group of 32 people
6 small groups (50 researchers) created for draft sections
Studied constitutions of USA, Germany, France, Japan, Lithuania and other states
Adopted concept of President's rule of law as basis

data.result: The Constitutional Commission was formed by the Supreme Council after the Declaration of Independence, initially with 64 members led by Karimov, later expanded to 71. It worked through specialized groups studying various constitutions and adopting the President's rule of law concept.

narr: Now let's look at how the Constitutional Commission was formed and operated.
When was the commission formed?
It was created after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence on June 20, 1990.
How was it initially composed?
The Supreme Council session created a commission of 64 people chaired by I. A. Karimov.
How did its composition change?
On July 2–3, 1992, the composition was updated to 71 members.
How did the commission work?
Direct work began on April 12, 1991 with a working group of 32 people.
What specialized structures were created?
Six small groups with 50 researchers total were created for different sections of the draft.
What materials did they study?
They studied constitutions of various countries including USA, Germany, France, Japan, and Lithuania.
What concept did they adopt?
From three alternative concepts, they adopted the concept of the President's rule of law as the basis.

data.heading: Question 3: Constitution Draft Versions
data.problem: What versions did the draft Constitution go through before publication?

Second version (spring 1992): 149 articles
Third version: 137 articles
Version for nationwide discussion: 127 articles
Initially prepared in Russian, then translated into Uzbek

data.result: The draft Constitution evolved through multiple versions: first with 158 articles, then 149, then 137, finally 127 for nationwide discussion. It was initially in Russian, then translated to Uzbek.

How many versions were there?

What was the first version like?
The first version from October-November 1991 contained 158 articles in six sections.
What about the second version?
In spring 1992, the second version was prepared with 149 articles.
And the third version?
The third version contained 137 articles.
What version was published for discussion?
For nationwide discussion, a version of 127 articles was published.
In what language was the draft prepared?
The project was initially prepared in Russian, then translated into Uzbek in July-August 1992.

data.heading: Question 4: Nationwide Discussion
data.problem: How did the nationwide discussion of the draft Constitution proceed?

steps.text: Commission comprehensively discussed the project on September 5, 1992
Published in press on September 26, 1992
Discussion occurred from late September to early December 1992
Took place in press, radio, television, labor collectives, and student auditoriums
Received over 6,000 proposals/comments and over 1,000 letters
Corrections made to 60 of 127 articles, 4 articles excluded
Second publication on November 21, 1992 established precedent of two-stage discussion

data.result: The nationwide discussion occurred from September to December 1992 across media and public venues, resulting in over 6,000 proposals and the establishment of a two-stage discussion process with a second publication.

narr: Now let's explore how the nationwide discussion of the draft Constitution proceeded.
When did the commission discuss the project?
The commission comprehensively discussed the project on September 5, 1992.
When was it first published?
It was published in the press on September 26, 1992.
When did the public discussion take place?
The discussion occurred from late September to early December 1992.
In what venues did the discussion happen?
It took place in the press, on radio and television, in labor collectives and student auditoriums.
How much public feedback was received?
The commission received over 6,000 proposals and comments and more than a thousand letters.
What changes were made based on feedback?
Corrections were made to 60 of the 127 articles, and 4 articles were excluded.
What precedent was established?
The second publication on November 21, 1992 established a precedent of two-stage discussion.

data.heading: Question 5: Key Constitutional Norms
data.problem: What key norms were included in the Constitution as a result of the discussion?

steps.text: Article 26 — presumption of innocence
Article 27 — secrecy of correspondence and telephone conversations
Article 31 — freedom of conscience with prohibition of forced religious views
Transformation of Arbitration Court into Economic Court
Naming parliament as the Oliy Majlis
Addition to Article 64 (now 65): 'Motherhood and childhood are under the protection of the state'

data.result: Key additions included presumption of innocence, privacy protections, freedom of conscience, court reorganization, parliamentary naming, and state protection for motherhood and childhood.

narr: Let's examine the key norms that were included in the Constitution as a result of the public discussion.
What rights were added regarding criminal procedure?
At the chairman's proposal, Article 26 was added establishing the presumption of innocence.
What privacy protections were included?
Article 27 was added guaranteeing the secrecy of correspondence and telephone conversations.
What religious freedom provisions were added?
Article 31 was added establishing freedom of conscience, stating that everyone has the right to believe or not believe in any religion, and forced imposition of religious views is not permitted.
How was the judicial system reorganized?
The Arbitration Court was transformed into an Economic Court.
What was the parliament renamed?
The parliament was named the Oliy Majlis.
What social protection provision was added?
At deputy Khalimakhon Usmonova's proposal, 'Motherhood and childhood are under the protection of the state' was added to Article 64 (now 65).

data.heading: Question 6: Rejected Constitutional Proposals
data.problem: What proposals were rejected during the preparation and adoption of the Constitution?

steps.text: Bicameral Oliy Majlis (Chamber of Representatives and Chamber of Nations)
Idea of bicameralism was only returned to later during second convocation
Norm on suspension of President's party membership (draft Article 90)
Membership in trade unions (contrary to voluntary nature of associations)
Appointment of prosecutors with consent of khokims

data.result: Rejected proposals included bicameral parliament (later implemented), presidential party membership suspension, mandatory trade union membership, and local prosecutor appointments.

narr: Now let's look at some proposals that were rejected during the Constitution's preparation and adoption.
What legislative structure was rejected?
The commission rejected the proposal for a bicameral Oliy Majlis with Chamber of Representatives and Chamber of Nations.
When was this idea reconsidered?
The idea of bicameralism was only returned to later, during the second convocation.
What presidential provision was excluded?
At the meeting on December 7, 1992, the norm on the suspension of the President's party membership was excluded from draft Article 90.
What organizational membership was not supported?
Membership in trade unions was not supported due to its contradiction with the voluntary nature of associations.
How was the prosecutor's office structured?

The proposal for appointing prosecutors with the consent of khokims was rejected; the prosecutor's office remained based on the principle of unity of command with all prosecutors appointed by the Prosecutor General.

data.heading: Question 7: Historical Justice Administration
data.problem: How was justice administered in ancient times and in the Bukhara and Khiva Khanates?

steps.text: 'Avesta' contained rules about judicial cases determining guilt, claim validity, and punishment
Various ancient peoples (Sakas, Kangyue, Huns, Sarmatians, Karluk, Turkic Khaganates) had their own legal systems
Under Muslim law, a single judge handled all criminal and family-inheritance cases
In khanates, head of judicial power was the emir and khan
Only the khan could pass a death sentence
Other officials (kushbegi, beks, qazi-kalon, qazi-askar) had rights except right to life and death

data.result: Historical justice administration evolved from ancient Avesta rules through various legal systems to centralized khanate authority where only the ruler could impose death sentences.

narr: Let's explore how justice was administered in ancient times and in the Bukhara and Khiva Khanates.
What early legal sources existed?
Already in the 'Avesta' there were rules about judicial cases determining guilt, claim validity, and punishment.
What legal systems existed among ancient peoples?
Among the Sakas, Kangyue, Huns, Sarmatians, Karluk and Turkic Khaganates, their own legal systems operated.
How was justice administered under Muslim law?
According to Muslim law, a single judge handled all criminal and family-inheritance cases.
Who headed the judicial system in the khanates?
In the khanates, the head of the judicial power was the emir and khan.
Who had authority to impose death sentences?
Only the khan could pass a death sentence.
What authority did other judicial officials have?
The kushbegi, beks, qazi-kalon and qazi-askar had rights except the right to life and death.

data.heading: Question 8: Russian Empire's Judicial System
data.problem: What judicial system did the Russian Empire introduce in Turkestan?

steps.text: 'Temporary Provision' of 1865 defined procedure for introducing imperial justice
'Draft Provision' of 1867 introduced two-tier court system
'Provision on the Administration of the Turkestan Region' approved on June 12, 1886 became main legal document
General courts and courts based on Sharia operated in parallel
For nomadic population, courts of qazis and biys were preserved
District judge performed dual function

data.result: The Russian Empire introduced a structured judicial system in Turkestan through multiple provisions, establishing parallel general and Sharia courts while preserving some traditional elements for nomadic populations.

narr: Finally, let's examine the judicial system introduced by the Russian Empire in Turkestan.
What early provisions established the imperial justice system?
The 'Temporary Provision' of 1865 defined the procedure for introducing imperial justice.
What structural changes did the 'Draft Provision' of 1867 introduce?
The 'Draft Provision' of 1867 introduced a two-tier court system.
What became the main legal document?
The 'Provision on the Administration of the Turkestan Region', approved by the emperor on June 12, 1886, became the main legal document.
How were different legal systems accommodated?
General courts and courts based on Sharia operated in parallel.
How was justice administered to nomadic populations?
For the nomadic population, the courts of qazis and biys were preserved.
What special role did district judges have?
The district judge performed a dual function.
